html:
Manillas were horseshoe-shaped bracelets of brass, bronze or copper used as money in West Africa from about 1500 until 1949. They were made in Europe by the millions and are closely tied to the Atlantic slave trade.

Copper and brass were already prized in West Africa when Portuguese traders arrived in the 15th century. They brought metal rings to trade for pepper, ivory and people, and later Dutch and English makers in places like Bristol and Birmingham turned them out in huge numbers. On parts of the coast, especially around the Niger delta and Calabar, prices of enslaved people were reckoned in manillas.

African smiths also melted them down. In 2023 a study of the metal showed that many of the Benin Bronzes were cast from brass manillas made in the German Rhineland.

Manillas stayed in use alongside cowrie shells and coins long after the slave trade ended. In colonial Nigeria the British bought them up and withdrew them in 1948 and 1949. Today they are worn as ornaments and kept as symbols of wealth.
sum: Manillas were horseshoe-shaped bracelets of brass, bronze or copper used as money in West Africa from about 1500 until 1949. They were made in Europe by the millions and are closely tied to the Atlantic slave trade.
